explanation: The PTO's 'standard operating speed' refers specifically to the rotational speed (RPM) at which the power-transfer output shaft itself turns, since implements are matched to that standardized shaft speed rather than to engine or gearbox RPM.

The differential lock forces both drive wheels to spin at the same rate, so it should be engaged when one wheel loses traction and spins freely while the other still has grip, allowing the tractor to keep moving instead of getting stuck.

Once the differential is locked, both wheels are forced to rotate at identical speeds, so turning the steering wheel while locked prevents the wheels from turning at the different rates a turn requires and can damage the drivetrain or cause loss of control.
A tractor's hitched attachments and additional equipment are powered through the hydraulic system, which delivers pressurized oil via hoses to operate the tool's cylinders and mechanisms.
Disconnecting hydraulic connectors while oil is still under pressure can cause it to spray out forcefully and injure the operator, so pressure must be confirmed as released before disengaging them.
With the engine off, cycling the operating lever through all its positions bleeds off any residual pressure trapped in the hydraulic lines safely, before the supply piping is disconnected.

A spark arrestor is required when the exhaust exits low near the ground, since hot sparks at that height can easily ignite dry grass, stubble, or fuel; an upper exhaust directs sparks safely away from combustible material.
Unhitching should be done on level ground because once the connection is released there is nothing holding the tool or trailer in place, and any slope could let it roll away unexpectedly.
Any tractor built with an enclosed driver's compartment must be fitted with front and rear direction indicators under the traffic regulations, regardless of whether it is mainly used off-road.

The middle lift arm (top link) of the three-point hitch stabilizes the implement against side-to-side swinging during operation, which also keeps the attached tool from pulling the tractor off its course.

After hitching a tool to the lift arms, the stabilizer chains or bars must be tightened to eliminate horizontal (side-to-side) play in the arms and tool, since uncontrolled swinging during transport is a hazard.

On a long, steep descent, relying solely on the wheel brakes can cause them to overheat and fail, so the safe method is to select a low gear beforehand and let the engine's compression control the descent speed.

The legal definition of an Autobus requires both a minimum passenger capacity of at least 8 besides the driver and formal classification as an Autobus in the vehicle's registration documents, not just its actual use.
A 'private Autobus' meets the general bus definition but is not operated as a service open to the general public, distinguishing it from a public transport bus.
The maximum number of passengers any registered public vehicle, including a minibus, may carry is fixed by and stated in its official registration documents, not by seat count or belts alone.
The regulatory definition caps a minibus's permitted gross (all-up) weight at 5,000 kg, which is what separates it in law from a full-size bus.
A 'touring vehicle' is legally defined as a public vehicle built to carry up to eight passengers besides the driver, provided it is specifically designated as such in its registration documents.

Because buses are heavy and slow to maneuver, they are barred from crossing where there is no solid asphalt or cement approach for at least 20 meters before the tracks, since a poor surface raises the risk of the bus stalling on the crossing.

The same surface-approach safety concern applies to any vehicle carrying or designed to carry at least 11 passengers besides the driver, which is barred from crossing where there is no paved road within 20 meters of the tracks.

When a bus stops before a level crossing under the stop-sign requirement, the driver must also open the front door, which improves the driver's ability to see and hear an approaching train before proceeding.

Safety shoes (wheel chocks) are required on motor vehicles above 5,000 kg gross weight to stop them rolling when parked, but buses fall under their own separate safety requirements and are excluded from this particular rule.
Absent a sign restricting the space to a specific vehicle type, ordinary parking rules apply equally to a small bus as to any other vehicle, so it may use the space like anyone else.
The sign shown follows the blue-background convention used for direction signs pointing to destinations on urban roads, distinguishing it from the green interurban and freeway direction signs.

Transporting school children legally requires a vehicle specifically authorized for that purpose, with the authorization noted in its registration documents, rather than any private or commercial vehicle with enough seats.
Decelerators and retarders exist to control speed on long descents without overheating the wheel brakes, so they must be used on any section preceded by a 'dangerous descent' warning sign.
Parking spaces designated for private vehicles are reserved for that vehicle class, so a bus carrying at least 20 passengers may not use them regardless of how many passengers are aboard.

A sign permitting parking on the sidewalk is intended for private vehicles, and a large bus authorized to carry at least 20 passengers is excluded from that allowance regardless of whether it currently has passengers.
As with other registered vehicles, the maximum passenger allowance for a desert vehicle is fixed by and stated in its official registration documents rather than by seat count or insurance terms.
Israeli licensing rules require a Class D license to drive buses or commercial vehicles with a gross weight over 3,500 kg, distinguishing them from the standard Class B private-car license.
A bus driver may only carry the number of passengers stated in the bus's registration documents, if such a figure is indicated there, rather than a generic fixed number.
A minibus driver holding a taxi license is legally capped at sixteen passengers besides the driver, regardless of how many seats the vehicle actually has.
Because public vehicles carry higher passenger-safety risk, the law requires their brakes to be inspected at a licensed garage at least every six months, more frequently than for private vehicles.

Traffic Regulation 97 requires both front lights to be functioning during lighting time, so if one headlight fails the vehicle no longer meets the mandatory lighting requirement and the driver must stop rather than continue.
Public transport operators have a legal duty to carry any paying passenger who boards, so running out of printed tickets for a route does not exempt the driver from providing the ride.
The law protects passenger comfort by obliging the driver to turn down the radio and shut off passenger loudspeakers whenever any single passenger requests it, not only when a majority agrees.
Bus drivers and conductors are legally required to behave politely and courteously toward passengers as a baseline standard of conduct.

A bus driver may only speak with passengers about matters relevant to the journey and must keep his attention and gaze on the road, since turning away to converse would compromise safe vehicle control.

Handling tickets or making change requires manual and visual attention that the driver cannot safely divert from driving, so selling tickets or giving change is prohibited while the vehicle is moving.
To protect passengers and maintain accountability, a public vehicle driver must show identification whenever any passenger requests it, not only officials or inspectors.
A first aid kit is mandatory equipment on a city-route passenger bus so that minor injuries can be treated on board.

Because conditions can change during a trip, the responsibility for a bus's security check rests with the driver continuously, both before departure and throughout the ride, not just at one fixed point.

The official maximum-speed table for buses other than minibuses sets 50 km/h in urban areas, 80 km/h on non-urban roads, 90 km/h on a non-urban road with a built median divider, and 100 km/h on a freeway.
The legal duty to announce upcoming stations specifically applies when the bus lacks a posted route map, since passengers then have no other way to track their location along the route.
Regardless of the bus's size, the law sets a floor of at least two glass-breaking hammers on board so passengers always have an emergency egress tool within reach.

A stretcher is required specifically on excursion or sightseeing buses, reflecting the greater risk of injury and distance from immediate medical help on longer touring trips, unlike ordinary city or regular-route buses.
The legal obligation to make change for a fare is capped at banknotes worth up to ten times the price of the ride, protecting the driver from being forced to break unreasonably large bills.
Checking that a bus's brakes, steering, horn, wipers, and doors function properly is the driver's own responsibility before every ride, not something delegated to a licensing facility or dispatcher.
A bus driver has the authority to refuse boarding to a passenger whose clothing could contaminate the seats, in order to protect the vehicle's condition and other passengers' comfort.

The law permits carrying cooking gas tanks on a certified tour bus only under strict limits, on an excursion only, up to two tanks of a maximum 12 kg each, stowed on the roof or rear trunk area to minimize fire risk.
Only the fixed, approved seats built into a bus or taxi may be used, because add-on chairs are not anchored or crash-tested for passenger safety.
A tachograph is mandatory equipment on a route-service bus so that driving and rest times can be recorded and enforced.
The two front seats beside the aisle on an inter-urban route bus are designated for security personnel, given their duty to respond quickly if needed.
A route-service bus driver may only load and unload passengers at the stations specified in the route license, not at any convenient point along the road.
Displaying the correct route signs on a service bus is the direct responsibility of the driver before each trip.

Under the lighting regulations for heavy/route vehicles, buses are required to run with headlights on during the day every year between November 1st and March 31st, reflecting reduced winter visibility.
An approved waste basket next to every door is mandatory equipment on a passenger bus, supporting cleanliness at the points passengers actually use.
A taxi signals it is free to hire by having its meter light illuminated and displaying 'Available', the standard convention for hailing an unoccupied taxi.
Soliciting passengers at Ben Gurion Airport is banned outright to preserve the orderly, regulated taxi queue system in place there.
A license from the Controller of Road Transport authorizes exactly three categories of taxi ride: sharing ride, private ride, and sightseeing ride.
The fare exemption is narrowly limited to one child under 5 accompanied by a paying adult, not to multiple unaccompanied children.

Because a private taxi ride is exclusive to the person who ordered it, a driver may only add another passenger with that passenger's consent, and doing so must not add extra fare for the agreed destination.
Assisting passengers with luggage when needed is part of a taxi driver's expected service duty.
A school transport vehicle must display flashing lamps and identifying signs, and its authorization for this use must be recorded in the vehicle's registration documents, not just marked externally.

Identification plates for the taxi owner and driver must be installed on the inner part of both the left and right door frame-heads, so passengers on either side can verify who is operating the vehicle.
Air conditioning is a mandatory installation in taxis, reflecting a passenger-comfort and safety standard applied to all such vehicles.
A meter-based tariff includes the distance the taxi travels from its own location to reach the person who ordered the ride, not only the trip from pickup to destination.
Tariff 1 is legally defined as the standard day tariff applying from 05:30 until 21:00.
Only a qualified, authorized taxi-meter service provider may certify that a meter functions correctly after its seal has been disconnected, preventing unverified tampering with the fare mechanism.
A malfunctioning taxi meter must be brought to a certified taxi-meter repair provider specifically, since ordinary garages are not authorized to service the regulated fare instrument.
By legal definition a minibus is classified as a taxi and is subject to the same taxi regulations in full.
Taxis are granted a limited exception allowing them to stop briefly within no-stopping zones on urban roads specifically to let passengers off, an allowance that doesn't extend to interurban roads.
The same limited exception applies to loading passengers within a no-stopping zone, but only on urban roads, not on other road types.
The maximum number of passengers a taxi driver may carry is set by the figure indicated in the vehicle's registration documents, not by seat count or driver discretion.
A minibus driver is capped at the number of passengers stated in the vehicle's registration documents, but in no case more than ten.
Taxi fares are set centrally under the regulated tariff system, so an owner or driver has no authority to unilaterally change the ride fare.

When a bus stops for a reason other than the regular loading and unloading of passengers, such as letting off an inspector, it is bound by the ordinary stopping rules that apply to any vehicle, not the route-license station restrictions.
Small animals may be carried on a bus only if they can be held securely on the passenger's knees or in their hands, balancing accommodation of pets with the comfort and safety of other passengers.
The law requires a bus to be disinfected once a year as a routine hygiene measure, independent of its annual mechanical test.
A taxi sightseeing ride is legally defined as an exclusive ride reserved for the person who ordered it, undertaken specifically for the purpose of touring or sightseeing.
A 'special' taxi ride is defined as an exclusive ride reserved solely for the individual who ordered it, distinguishing it from a shared or route-service ride.
Refueling with passengers aboard risks fire or fume exposure to them, so it is prohibited whenever the bus is carrying passengers, regardless of the fuel type or station.
Transporting a passenger's wheelchair must be done free of charge under accessibility rules, without any added fare.

Keeping a safe gap from the vehicle ahead exists because that vehicle may brake suddenly and unpredictably, and only an adequate following distance gives the driver behind time to react and stop safely, independent of time of day or specific descent signs.
Without a valid taxi operation permit the vehicle cannot legally function as a taxi, so its meter, a taxi-specific fare instrument, must be removed to prevent illegal operation.
The children's fare rule for route-service taxis allows no more than two children under 5, seated on the knees of full-fare-paying adults, to ride free; beyond that limit a fare applies.
Tariff 2 is legally defined as the night/holiday tariff, applying from 21:01 until 05:29 and throughout the Sabbath and holidays.
A zotobus is defined by regulation as a taxi-class vehicle weighing between 2,200 and 3,500 kg and permitted to carry up to 10 passengers.
Legally, briefly halting to let passengers off is classified as 'stopping' rather than 'parking', since it is a short operational pause directly tied to passenger movement.
A bus driver who needs corrective lenses must carry a spare pair, ensuring that losing or damaging the primary glasses or contacts doesn't leave him unable to drive safely.
Buses are not restricted to bus lanes alone; like other vehicles, they may also use ordinary marked traffic lanes in addition to dedicated bus lanes.
The seat belt duty under the traffic regulations applies to a public minibus's driver and passengers on every type of road, with no road-type exemption.

Israeli traffic law grants a specific seat belt exemption to rear-seat taxi passengers on urban roads, reflecting the frequent, short-hop nature of city taxi trips, unlike interurban roads where the standard belt rule applies.
A taxi driver is exempt from wearing a seat belt only on urban roads and only while carrying passengers, reflecting the operational need to move freely for passenger service on shorter city trips.
Before pulling away from a stop, a bus driver must signal the direction of travel he is about to take, alerting following traffic in line with standard maneuver-signaling requirements.
A bus may only remain stopped at a bus stop for as long as it actually takes to load and unload passengers, not for an open-ended or arbitrary period.
The duty to carry passengers on a route-service bus is broad, extending to virtually anyone wishing to board, but it still remains subject to any other applicable statutory restrictions.
Public vehicles operate under a general duty to carry any passenger willing to pay the fare, reflecting their role as a service open to the public rather than at the driver's personal discretion.
On a route-service bus, one or two seats marked and positioned next to the entrance are reserved for handicapped passengers, giving them easier access.
Managing and being responsible for the safe entry and exit of passengers rests with the bus driver directly, not the vehicle owner or dispatcher.
Carrying passengers with loaded weapons is prohibited except for personnel on official duty, balancing public safety with the operational needs of security and defense personnel.
